cues.text: Chapter five is the practical design lab and troubleshooting.
This is where everything you have studied so far comes together in a hands-on project.
The capstone is a three-site secure monitored enterprise.
That means one headquarters, which we usually shorten to HQ, and two branch offices.
You will simulate the whole thing on Ubuntu, using four tools: GNS3, Mininet, pfSense and Open vSwitch.
GNS3 is a network simulator for building virtual topologies.
Mininet creates virtual hosts and switches on a single machine. pfSense is a firewall and router platform.
Open vSwitch is a virtual switch.
Together they let you build and test a realistic enterprise network without buying physical equipment.
Now, how do you begin?
Start on paper, before you touch any software.
First, draw a topology diagram, showing the three sites and how they connect.
Second, make an interface inventory, which is a list of every device interface that will be used.
Third, plan your subnets, meaning the address ranges for each part of the network.
Fourth, write a traffic and security matrix, which states which traffic is allowed and which is blocked between the different parts of the network.
Next comes configuration.
Configure the interfaces inside an isolated simulator, so that nothing you do can affect a real network.
Then test in a sensible order.
First, test same-subnet connectivity, meaning devices that sit on the same network talking directly to each other.
Second, test routed connectivity, meaning traffic that has to cross a router to reach another subnet.
Third, test policy, meaning that the rules you wrote in your security matrix really allow what they should allow and block what they should block.
And throughout, record actual observations only.
Write down what you really saw, not what you expected to see.
Here is an example of a Huawei VRP interface configuration.
The source notes that the syntax depends on the device, so treat this as an illustration, not a universal recipe.
Note too that this is a configuration example; it is not a record of it having been run.
The first command is system-view.
This moves you from user view into system view, which is the mode where you can change configuration.
The second is interface GigabitEthernet 0/0/0.
This selects the interface you want to configure: a Gigabit Ethernet interface, numbered zero slash zero slash zero.
The third, written with a leading space to show it sits inside that interface, is ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0.
This assigns the IP address 192.168.10.1 with the subnet mask 255.255.255.0.
That mask is equivalent to a slash 24 prefix, so the interface sits in the 192.168.10.0 network.
The fourth is undo shutdown.
In Huawei VRP, the word undo reverses a command.
So this cancels the shutdown state and brings the interface up.
The fifth is quit, which leaves the interface view.
The last command is display ip interface brief.
This shows a short summary of the IP interfaces, so you can check the address and status you just configured.
One important point: use a routed interface supported by the device.
Not every port on every device can take an IP address in this way, so check what your device and simulator actually support.
Now let us talk about troubleshooting.
Verify things in this order, as appropriate to the problem.
First, the physical link.
Second, the IP address and mask.
Third, the VLAN.
Fourth, the gateway.
Fifth, the route.
Sixth, the ACL, which is the access control list.
Seventh, DNS.
And finally, the application.
The logic is that each layer depends on the ones before it, so there is little point checking DNS if the cable is unplugged.
Be careful about what your tools tell you.
Ping tests ICMP reachability, and only that.
It does not prove that every service works.
A successful ping does not mean a web server or a database is functioning, and a firewall may block ICMP even when the service is fine.
Likewise, traceroute reveals some responding hops, but not necessarily a complete path.
Some devices do not respond, so gaps do not always mean a fault.
Finally, the tools for diagrams and simulation.
These include GNS3, Packet Tracer, eNSP, and draw.io-style diagrams.
The last of these is for drawing, while the others simulate.
The key rule is that the simulator must match the intended device capabilities.
If your design depends on a feature the simulator cannot reproduce, your results will not tell you how the real device would behave.
